checkpoints: Understand what a browser does when you type a URL
Learn the difference between HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
Set up VS Code with helpful extensions
Create your first HTML file and open it in a browser

content.value: Before writing a single line of React, you need a mental model of the web. When you type a URL, your browser sends a request to a server, which responds with HTML. The browser reads the HTML and constructs a tree of elements called the DOM (Document Object Model). CSS styles that tree, and JavaScript makes it interactive. React is simply a smarter way to manage and update that DOM. Understanding this foundation will make every React concept feel logical rather than magical.

checkpoints: Write semantic HTML with headings, paragraphs, lists, and links
Style elements using class selectors and the box model
Build a simple two-column layout using Flexbox
Make your layout responsive with media queries

content.value: HTML gives your page structure, CSS gives it style. Learn semantic tags like <header>, <main>, and <footer> — they matter for accessibility and SEO. The box model (margin, border, padding, content) controls spacing. Flexbox is the layout system you'll use constantly in React: it lets you align and distribute items in a row or column. Practice building a simple card or navigation bar. Responsive design with media queries ensures your UI works on mobile too.

checkpoints: Understand variables with let and const
Write functions using arrow function syntax
Use array methods: map, filter, and find
Destructure objects and arrays
Understand what a Promise is and how async/await works

content.value: React is JavaScript, so a firm foundation pays dividends immediately. Focus on modern ES6+ syntax: const and let instead of var, arrow functions, and template literals. The array method map() is central to React — you'll use it to render lists. Destructuring lets you unpack values cleanly: const { name, age } = user. Async/await is how you'll eventually fetch data from APIs. You don't need to master all of JavaScript before starting React, but these fundamentals will unlock 90% of what you need.

checkpoints: Create a project with Vite: npm create vite@latest
Understand the folder structure (src, public, index.html)
Write your first functional component
Return JSX and render the component in App.jsx

content.value: Use Vite to scaffold your project — it's fast and modern. Run npm create vite@latest, choose React, then npm install and npm run dev. Inside src/, App.jsx is your root component. A React component is just a JavaScript function that returns JSX — HTML-like syntax that React transforms into DOM elements. Components start with a capital letter. Your first goal: delete the boilerplate and render a heading with your name. Simple, but it confirms everything is wired correctly.

checkpoints: Pass data into a component using props
Use useState to track a value that changes
Build a simple counter that increments and decrements
Understand why state is separate from props

content.value: Props are how a parent component passes data to a child — they flow downward and are read-only. State is data that a component owns and can change. Use the useState hook: const [count, setCount] = useState(0). When you call setCount, React re-renders the component with the new value. Build a counter: a button that says +1 and another that says -1. This tiny project teaches the core React loop — event triggers state update, state update triggers re-render.

checkpoints: Render an array of items using .map() inside JSX
Add a unique key prop to each list item
Handle onClick events to respond to user interaction
Handle onChange on an input to capture text

content.value: Rendering a list in React means mapping an array to JSX elements. Each element needs a unique key prop so React can efficiently update the DOM. Events use camelCase: onClick, onChange, onSubmit. An input's value combined with onChange gives you controlled inputs — a pattern you'll use in every form. Try building a to-do list where you type a task, press a button, and see it added to a list below. This combines state, events, and list rendering into one practical mini-app.

checkpoints: Use a regular CSS file imported into your component
Apply inline styles using a JavaScript object
Install and use Tailwind CSS in your Vite project
Use conditional class names based on state

content.value: React gives you several ways to style components. Plain CSS files work fine for simple projects — just import './Button.css'. Inline styles are objects: style={{ color: 'red', fontSize: '16px' }}. Tailwind CSS is the most popular choice in modern React: utility classes like bg-blue-500 and rounded-xl let you style without leaving JSX. Try toggling a class based on state — for example, showing a green or red background on a button depending on whether a task is done.

checkpoints: Create a Header component with your name and navigation links
Create an About section component with a short bio
Create a Projects component that renders a list of project cards
Apply Tailwind CSS to make the page look polished
Deploy to Vercel or Netlify

content.value: Put everything together by building a personal portfolio. Break the page into components: Header, About, Projects, and Footer. Pass project data as props to a reusable ProjectCard component. Use Tailwind for layout and styling. This project exercises every beginner concept — components, props, lists, and styling — in a real context you can show to others. When you're happy with it, deploy it for free on Vercel. Sharing a live URL is far more memorable than showing screenshots.
